thunderstorm Atmospheric Physics

Can you discern the shape?

The thunder rumbles, the ground is wet, and a snake seeks shelter. In the chaos of the storm, you look closely at the rain...

visibility_off

The Short Answer: No.

You see streaks, not shapes.

Raindrops fall at speeds up to 10 meters per second (22 mph). The human eye has an "integration time" (similar to a camera's shutter speed) of roughly 0.1 seconds.

By the time your retina processes the image, the drop has fallen several meters, creating the visual illusion of a long, thin streak due to motion blurlink .

Why is the snake here?

It's not hunting you. Heavy rains flood underground dens and burrows, forcing snakes like the one you saw to seek higher, drier ground. Researchlink suggests they are also highly active during storms to hunt amphibians that emerge in the wet conditions.

💧

The Myth

"Teardrop" shape. Only happens when water drips from a faucet (due to adhesion), not in freefall.

🍔

The Reality

"Hamburger Bun" shape. Air pressure pushes up against the bottom, flattening it as speed increases.
